cosy-lesson.title: "A child has the right to be difficult, that is the only way they learn to be themselves.": Françoise Dolto

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: to introduce the topic and clarify key target vocabulary for the session.

cosy-slide.cosy-instruction: Review the key vocabulary for this session below:

cosy-blockquote.p: Independent – capable of thinking or acting on one's own without constant supervision.

p.em: Example: Encouraging children to make their own choices builds a highly independent mind.

cosy-blockquote.p: Boundaries – the limits or rules set to establish safe and respectful behavior in relationships.

p.em: Example: Setting clear parental boundaries helps children feel secure while learning self-control.

cosy-blockquote.p: Confident – feeling sure of one's own abilities, qualities, or ideas.

p.em: Example: A child who is allowed to disagree with their parents often grows into a highly confident adult.

cosy-blockquote.p: Respectful – showing politeness, care, and honor toward others and their rules.

p.em: Example: Children can learn to be respectful of others while still expressing their own opinions.

cosy-blockquote.p: Discipline – the practice of training people to obey rules or code of behavior.

p.em: Example: Traditional discipline often focused strictly on obedience rather than understanding.

cosy-blockquote.p: Stubborn – refusing to change one's mind or behavior despite argument or persuasion.

p.em: Example: His stubborn resistance to bedtime rules was actually a normal step in self-discovery.

cosy-blockquote.p: Curious – having a strong desire to learn, explore, or know about things.

p.em: Example: A highly curious child will constantly ask 'why' and test the limits of rules.

cosy-blockquote.p: Obedient – willing to comply with orders, rules, or requests from authority figures.

p.em: Example: While an obedient child is easy to manage, they might struggle to make independent choices later.

cosy-blockquote.p: Freedom – the power or right to act, speak, or think as one wants without hindrance.

p.em: Example: Giving children the freedom to make mistakes is essential for building confidence.

cosy-blockquote.p: Responsibility – the state or fact of having a duty to deal with something or of having control over oneself.

p.em: Example: With greater personal freedom comes the need to learn personal responsibility.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: pair/group discussion on core session themes.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs or small breakout groups, discuss the following questions:

ol.li:
Can a child build genuine independent thinking without sometimes disappointing or resisting adults?
★ Were you a stubborn or difficult child? What rules did you rebel against most?

Is it possible for parents to set healthy boundaries without demanding strict, unconditional obedient behavior?
★ Did your parents let you disagree with them openly, or did they expect you to be quiet and obedient?

How does having a confident voice as a child affect a person's future sense of responsibility?
★ What rule or parental discipline from your childhood are you most grateful for today?

Why are curious children often labeled as difficult or problematic in traditional classrooms?
★ How much freedom did your parents give you to explore your own hobbies and interests?

How can parents remain respectful of a child's unique personality when enforcing daily discipline?
★ Have you ever had to choose between showing respect to authority and staying true to your own freedom?

Does a child need absolute freedom of self-expression to develop into a highly independent adult?
★ Do you think modern children have too much freedom compared to your own childhood?

How should parents react when a child's natural curious nature clashes with school rules and discipline?
★ Can you recall a moment where your own curiosity led you to cross parental boundaries?

Why is teaching a child to be respectful of others sometimes confused with demanding they be completely obedient?
★ In what areas of your life do you feel you are most respectful of established boundaries today?

At what point does a parent's desire to raise a confident child lead to an attitude that lacks responsibility?
★ How has your own understanding of personal responsibility shifted over the last five years?

Is a child's stubborn refusal to conform actually a sign of healthy personal boundaries development?
★ If you had to describe your childhood relationship with parental discipline in one word, what would it be?

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: collaborative task or visual analysis in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, work together on the following task:

cosy-blockquote.p: Which child profile below is most likely to develop into the happiest, most successful adult? Rank them and explain your reasoning to your partner: - 😇 Profile A: The Compliant Learner Always obeyed rules, never argued, and stayed quiet to avoid any conflict with authority. - 🔥 Profile B: The Stubborn Rebel Often questioned rules, made many mistakes, but always stood up for their personal freedom. - 🧠 Profile C: The Curious Explorer Highly stubborn, deeply curious about everything, occasionally crossed parental boundaries. - 💼 Profile D: The Disciplined Thinker Showed strong self-discipline, stayed respectful of rules, but struggled to express feelings.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: 1-on-1 guided visual description and task response with teacher.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: deeper debate and statement evaluation in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, debate and state whether you agree or disagree with these statements:

ol.li:
In the future, school systems will reward independent, rebellious thinking far more than traditional academic compliance. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ How would you adapt if school rules became completely flexible, allowing children unlimited freedom?

Future parents will allow children to question every single household rule, making traditional discipline obsolete. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Would you be willing to use AI parenting assistants to set personalized boundaries for future generations?

Future societies will view a stubborn child as a highly positive sign of leadership potential. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ How do you want future generations of your family to remember your approach to personal freedom?

As technology advances, children will be given full financial responsibility at a much younger age. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ If you could design a futuristic school, how would you teach the value of personal responsibility to children?

In the coming decades, demanding children be obedient to adults will be seen as a violation of their rights. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Do you fear a future where children's behavior is fully managed or monitored by school algorithms?

The survival of future human society will depend on raising highly curious minds who reject conformity. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ How do you personally prepare for a future where true curious exploration is increasingly rare?

Future generations will look back at today's strict classroom discipline with deep skepticism and shock. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ If you could send a single message about raising a confident child to people living 100 years in the future, what would it be?

Global digital connectivity will make it incredibly easy for children to build independent projects online. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Would you choose to live in a futuristic community that completely guarantees children's safety at the cost of their freedom?

In the future, social status will be determined by how confident a person is rather than their family wealth. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ What role do you hope personal boundaries will play in your own professional future over the next decade?

A future world governed fully by smart technology will leave no space left for children to learn responsibility through mistakes. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ If a parenting app could perfectly teach a child to be respectful, would you still value human guidance?

ul.li: Incorrect: He have went to Paris → Correct: He has gone to Paris ((Present perfect third-person singular 'has' + past participle 'gone'.))

Incorrect: We discussed about the problem → Correct: We discussed the problem / had a discussion about the problem (('Discuss' is transitive and takes no preposition, or use 'have a discussion about'.))
Incorrect: I am agree with you → Correct: I agree with you ((Use 'agree' directly as a verb rather than using it with the auxiliary 'am'.))
